citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median (middle) lobe... Its upper surface is related to the trigone of the bladder; it is rich in glands.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
coreConcept: Post-void Residual and the Uvula Vesicae
statement: A 65-year-old patient with long-standing urinary obstruction due to median lobe hypertrophy is found to have a 'pouch' of stagnant urine in the bladder. Anatomically, where is this pouch specifically located and why does it form?
options: Lateral to the ureteric orifices due to lateral lobe atrophy
Within the prostatic utricle due to ejaculatory duct obstruction
Behind the urethral orifice due to the enlargement of the uvula vesicae
Anterior to the urethral orifice due to anterior lobe fibrosis
Superior to the trigone due to relaxation of the detrusor muscle
correctOption: Behind the urethral orifice due to the enlargement of the uvula vesicae
optionExplanations: Lateral lobes cause urethral compression but do not typically create the specific retro-urethral pouch described; BPH involves hyperplasia, not atrophy.
The prostatic utricle is too small to hold significant stagnant urine and is located within the urethra, not the bladder.

The median lobe's upward growth elevates the uvula vesicae (a small elevation in the trigone). This creates a mechanical basin behind the internal urethral orifice where urine collects and cannot be easily expelled.
The anterior lobe is non-glandular and does not enlarge in BPH to create such a pouch.
The detrusor usually undergoes compensatory hypertrophy (not relaxation) in early obstruction, and the pouch is a mechanical consequence of lobe growth, not muscle tone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The enlargement of the uvula vesicae (owing to the enlarged median lobe) results in the formation of a pouch of stagnant urine behind the urethral orifice within the bladder.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: A 72-year-old male with confirmed prostatic carcinoma presents with new-onset lower back pain. Radiographs reveal osteoblastic lesions in the lumbar vertebrae. Which anatomical feature of the prostatic venous drainage best explains this clinical progression?
options: The plexus drains exclusively into the internal pudendal vein
The plexus has no connection to the pelvic bones
The plexus is located inside the fibrous capsule
The dorsal vein of the penis prevents reverse flow
The veins are thin-walled and valveless
correctOption: The veins are thin-walled and valveless
optionExplanations: The plexus drains into the internal iliac veins, not just the internal pudendal, and more importantly, it connects to the vertebral system.
The plexus has extensive connections to the vertebral veins and pelvic bones, which explains why the lower column is a frequent site for skeletal metastases.
The prostatic venous plexus actually lies outside the capsule of the prostate, though this location is secondary to the physiological nature of the flow.
The deep dorsal vein of the penis actually drains into the prostatic plexus; it does not serve as a valve to prevent metastasis to the vertebrae.

The prostatic venous plexus is valveless. During periods of increased intra-abdominal pressure (coughing/straining), blood can flow retrogradely into the vertebral venous plexus, carrying malignant cells directly to the axial skeleton.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The veins have thin walls, are valveless, and are drained by several large trunks directly into the internal iliac veins... it is possible for prostatic venous blood to flow in a reverse direction and enter the vertebral veins.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: In a patient with acute urinary retention, a catheter is passed through the male urethra. Upon reaching the prostatic portion, the clinician recalls that this segment has unique physical properties compared to the membranous part. What is the primary characteristic of the prostatic urethra?
options: It is roughly 6 inches (15 cm) long.
It is the narrowest part of the entire urethra.
It contains the openings of the bulbourethral glands.
It is the least dilatable portion of the urethra.
It is the widest and most dilatable portion of the entire urethra.
correctOption: It is the widest and most dilatable portion of the entire urethra.
optionExplanations: 6 inches is the length of the penile (spongy) urethra; the prostatic urethra is only about 1.25 inches long.
The external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans penis is the narrowest part of the male urethra.
The ducts of the bulbourethral glands open into the penile (spongy) urethra, just below the perineal membrane, not in the prostatic segment.
The intermediate (membranous) part of the urethra is the least dilatable because it is surrounded by the rigid perineal membrane and the external sphincter.
The prostatic urethra is the widest and most flexible/dilatable part of the male urethra, allowing for easier passage of larger instruments once the bladder neck is reached.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The prostatic urethra is about 1.25 in. (3 cm) long and begins at the neck of the bladder. ... The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable portion of the entire urethra.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
coreConcept: Embryological homology of the prostatic utricle
statement: In the prostatic urethra, a longitudinal ridge called the urethral crest is found on the posterior wall. What is the clinical significance of the prostatic utricle located on this crest?
options: It is the female homologue of the uterus and vagina.
It is the specific site for the entry of mature sperm into the urethra.
It contains the sphincter mechanism for urinary continence.
It is the opening for the two bulbourethral glands.
It is the site where the prostatic glands discharge their alkaline secretions.
correctOption: It is the female homologue of the uterus and vagina.
optionExplanations: The prostatic utricle is a vestigial remnant of the paramesonephric ducts, which in the female form the uterus and vagina.
Mature sperm enter through the ejaculatory ducts, which open on the margins of the mouth of the utricle, but the utricle itself does not transport sperm.
The sphincter mechanism (sphincter vesicae) is at the neck of the bladder, superior to the verumontanum and utricle.
Bulbourethral glands open into the penile (spongy) urethra, not the prostatic portion.
The prostatic glands open into the prostatic sinuses on either side of the urethral crest, not specifically into the utricle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A small depression, the prostatic utricle (which is an analog of the uterus and vagina in females) lies on the summit of the urethral crest.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: Which specific lobe of the prostate gland is primarily associated with the clinical presentation of early stage malignancy that is typically detected as a hard nodule during a digital rectal examination?
optionExplanations: The median or middle lobe is a wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts; its enlargement is associated with BPH and uvula vesicae rather than palpable rectal nodules.
The lateral lobes lie on either side of the urethra and are separated by a shallow vertical groove, but the posterior lobe is the primary surface explored during rectal palpation.
While lateral lobes contain many glands, they are not the primary posterior surface where clinicians initially detect hard malignant nodules via rectal exam.
The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and is described as being devoid of glandular tissue, making it a rare site for carcinoma or clinically significant nodules.

The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts. It is the part of the gland felt through the anterior rectal wall during a digital rectal exam, where malignant nodules typically originate.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts and also contains glandular tissue.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: An anatomical assessment of the prostate gland is performed to differentiate between its various subdivisions. Which of the following lobes is characterized by a complete absence of glandular tissue and lies anterior to the urethra?
optionExplanations: The posterior lobe is located behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts; it contains significant glandular tissue and is a common site for primary carcinoma development.
The left lateral lobe, similar to its right counterpart, is rich in glands and separated from the right lobe by a shallow vertical groove on the posterior surface.

The anterior lobe is unique among the five prostatic lobes because it is primarily fibromuscular and lacks the glandular elements responsible for prostatic secretions, serving mainly as a structural boundary in front of the urethra.
The right lateral lobe is one of the primary masses of the gland situated on the side of the urethra; it is highly glandular and often involved in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
The median lobe is a wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts; it is actually very rich in glandular tissue and contributes to the uvula vesicae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and is devoid of glandular tissue.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: A clinician identifies the level of the internal urethral orifice during a procedure. Which prostatic structure is situated immediately behind this orifice and is responsible for the formation of the uvula vesicae?
optionExplanations: The median lobe is a wedge of glandular tissue between the urethra and ejaculatory ducts; its superior surface is directly related to the bladder trigone, forming the uvula vesicae.
The posterior lobe is situated inferior to the ejaculatory ducts and is separated from the bladder by the median lobe and ejaculatory ducts.
The prostatic apex is the most inferior part of the gland, resting on the urogenital diaphragm, far from the internal urethral orifice at the bladder neck.
The lateral lobes are situated on either side of the urethra and do not form the midline uvula vesicae elevation.
The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and has no relationship to the posterior aspect of the urethral orifice or the bladder trigone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The uvula vesicae are a small elevation situated immediately behind the urethral orifice, which is produced by the underlying median lobe of the prostate.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A 70-year-old male presents with a frequent and intense reflex desire to micturate, which his physician attributes to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). According to the pathophysiological mechanism of the gland, what anatomical event triggers this specific reflex?
options: Atrophy of the prostatic venous plexus
Compression of the internal iliac artery
Encroachment of the anterior lobe on the symphysis pubis
Leakage of urine into the prostatic urethra
correctOption: Leakage of urine into the prostatic urethra
optionExplanations: Ejaculatory ducts are related to the median and posterior lobes but their dilation does not trigger the urge to urinate.
Atrophy is not associated with BPH; rather, the venous plexus is often congested and represents a risk for hemorrhage.
The internal iliac artery provides the blood supply but its compression does not trigger the micturition reflex.
The anterior lobe is devoid of glandular tissue and its enlargement is not the primary cause of micturition symptoms in BPH.
When the median lobe enlarges, it disrupts the sphincter vesicae, allowing urine to leak into the prostatic urethra, which initiates the micturition reflex.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median lobe of the gland enlarges upward and encroaches within the sphincter vesicae, located at the neck of the bladder (Fig. 9.17). The leakage of urine into the prostatic urethra causes an intense reflex desire to micturate.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: A clinical pathologist is analyzing prostatic fluid obtained from a patient. The presence of high concentrations of acid phosphatase is noted. Which anatomical component of the prostate is the primary source of this enzyme?
options: The smooth muscle fibers of the capsule
The stratified squamous lining of the prostatic utricle
The connective tissue of the rectoprostatic fascia
The glandular epithelial cells of the median and lateral lobes
correctOption: The glandular epithelial cells of the median and lateral lobes
optionExplanations: Smooth muscle fibers in the prostate are responsible for contracting to squeeze the secretion out, but they do not produce the enzyme themselves.
The prostatic utricle is a developmental remnant and not the primary source of the enzymes found in prostatic fluid.
The rectoprostatic fascia (Denonvilliers') is a supportive connective tissue layer and lacks secretory function.
The anterior lobe is devoid of glandular tissue and therefore cannot be the source of acid phosphatase.

Acid phosphatase is synthesized and secreted by the glandular epithelial cells that make up the bulk of the median, posterior, and lateral lobes. Its level in the blood rises if these cells cannot discharge secretion into the ducts.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The numerous glands of the prostate are embedded in a mixture of smooth muscle and connective tissue... Acid phosphatase is an important enzyme present in the secretion in large amounts.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A surgical approach to the prostate requires a precise understanding of its apical and basal relations. Which of the following correctly describes the relationship of the prostate's apex and base to surrounding structures?
options: The apex is continuous with the internal urethral sphincter.
The apex lies against the upper surface of the urogenital diaphragm.
The apex is continuous with the neck of the bladder.
The base is related to the retropubic pad of fat.
The base lies against the superior surface of the urogenital diaphragm.
correctOption: The apex lies against the upper surface of the urogenital diaphragm.
optionExplanations: The internal urethral sphincter is at the bladder neck, making it continuous with the base of the prostate, not the apex.
The prostate is inverted-conical in shape. The narrow lower end (apex) rests on the urogenital diaphragm (specifically the superior fascia thereof).
Incorrect. The base of the prostate (the superior surface) is continuous with the neck of the bladder.
The anterior surface of the prostate is related to the retropubic fat, not the base (which is superior).
Incorrect. The base is the superior part of the gland; the apex is the inferior part that rests on the diaphragm.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The somewhat conical prostate has a base, which lies against the bladder neck above, and an apex, which lies against the urogenital diaphragm below.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: During a digital rectal examination (DRE), a clinician palpates the prostate to assess for malignancy. Which lobe is primarily accessible through the anterior rectal wall?
optionExplanations: Palpating only the left lateral lobe would indicate an incomplete examination or unilateral pathology, not the general anatomical accessibility.
The anterior lobe is separated from the rectum by the urethra and the entire mass of the gland; it cannot be palpated via rectum.
The lateral lobes are palpated as part of the overall mass, but the specific lobe forming the posterior surface is the posterior lobe.
The median lobe is situated too superiorly and deep within the gland to be the primary lobe felt on DRE.
Correct. The posterior lobe is the part of the gland situated behind the urethra and is the portion felt directly through the anterior wall of the rectal ampulla during DRE.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts and also contains glandular tissue.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
coreConcept: Prostate Lobe Classification and Histological Composition
statement: Anatomical examination of the prostate gland reveals that one of its five lobes is uniquely characterized by a complete absence of glandular tissue. Which of the following lobes corresponds to this description?
optionExplanations: The median (middle) lobe is a wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts and is described as being rich in glands.
The right lateral lobe is one of the two main glandular masses on either side of the urethra and is rich in prostatic glands.
The anterior lobe of the prostate is primarily fibromuscular and is distinct because it lacks glandular components entirely, unlike the other four lobes.
The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts and contains functional glandular tissue.
The left lateral lobe, similar to the right, contains many glands and is separated from its counterpart by a shallow vertical groove posteriorly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and is devoid of glandular tissue.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: In the internal anatomy of the prostate, which lobe is described as a glandular wedge specifically localized between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts?
optionExplanations: The lateral lobes are located on the sides of the urethra, not specifically wedged between the urethra and the ducts.
The posterior lobe is located behind the urethra but specifically inferior to (below) the ejaculatory ducts.
The anterior lobe is located in front of the urethra, not between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts.
The peripheral zone is a histological/radiological classification, not one of the five incomplete anatomical lobes described in the gross anatomy text.
The median lobe is the specific wedge of glandular tissue that occupies the space between the prostatic urethra and the two ejaculatory ducts.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median (middle) lobe is the wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A 60-year-old male with Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) reports constant 'dribbling' and an intense reflex desire to micturate. Anatomical analysis shows that his median lobe has enlarged upward. Which internal bladder structure is most likely distorted to produce the 'uvula vesicae' elevation and subsequent urinary stasis?
optionExplanations: The interureteric ridge limits the trigone superiorly but is not the site of the uvula vesicae.
The median lobe of the prostate lies directly beneath the trigone. Its hypertrophy pushes the trigone upward, creating the uvula vesicae and a post-prostatic pouch for stagnant urine.
The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the urachus and is far removed from the prostatic base.
The ureteric orifices are the lateral angles of the trigone, not the midline site of prostatic encroachment.
The apex of the bladder is anterior, related to the symphysis pubis and the urachus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median (middle) lobe is the wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts. Its upper surface is related to the trigone of the bladder; it is rich in glands. ... The enlargement of the uvula vesicae (owing to the enlarged median lobe) results in the formation of a pouch of stagnant urine behind the urethral orifice

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: A patient diagnosed with prostatic carcinoma is found to have skeletal metastases in the lower vertebral column. Which anatomical feature of the prostatic venous drainage facilitates this specific route of spread during episodes of increased intra-abdominal pressure?
options: The fusion of the rectovesical septum with the sacral periosteum.
Direct lymphatic drainage from the posterior lobe to the lumbar nodes.
The high-pressure system within the inferior vesical artery reversing flow.
The deep dorsal vein of the penis draining directly into the internal iliac vein.
Valveless connections between the prostatic plexus and vertebral veins.
correctOption: Valveless connections between the prostatic plexus and vertebral veins.
optionExplanations: The rectovesical septum (Denonvilliers' fascia) separates the prostate from the rectum, it does not provide a direct pathway for skeletal metastasis.
Prostatic lymph drains to internal iliac nodes, not directly to lumbar nodes; the lumbar spread described in the case is typically hematogenous.
Arterial systems do not typically reverse flow to provide a pathway for cancer spread; this is a function of the low-pressure venous system.
The deep dorsal vein does drain into the prostatic plexus, but this is the normal direction of flow and does not explain the spread to the spine.

The prostatic venous plexus is linked to the Batson venous plexus (vertebral veins). These veins are valveless, meaning increased abdominal pressure (coughing, straining) can force blood (and cancer cells) backward into the vertebral system, leading to spinal metastases.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Many connections exist between the prostatic venous plexus and the vertebral veins. During coughing and sneezing or abdominal straining, it is possible for prostatic venous blood to flow in a reverse direction and enter the vertebral veins.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A physician performing a digital rectal examination (DRE) palpates a hard nodule on the prostate. Anatomically, which surface and lobe are being assessed through the anterior wall of the rectal ampulla?
optionExplanations: The anterior surface and lobe are separated from the rectum by the urethra and the bulk of the gland, making them inaccessible via DRE.
The superior surface (base) is in contact with the bladder; while the median lobe is near the base, it is not the primary lobe palpated during a standard DRE.
The posterior surface of the prostate, which corresponds to the posterior lobe, lies directly anterior to the rectum, separated only by the rectovesical septum, making it the primary area palpated.
The apex is the most inferior part of the gland, but it is not a 'surface' and is less clinically significant for nodule palpation than the posterior surface.
The lateral lobes are palpated to the sides, but the standard 'nodule' assessment described in clinical scenarios refers to the posterior lobe palpated through the rectal wall.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The examiner’s gloved finger can feel the posterior surface of the prostate through the anterior rectal wall. ... The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
coreConcept: Morphological lobar anatomy of the prostate and its relations to the bladder trigone.
statement: Which morphological segment of the prostate gland is described as a wedge situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts, with its superior surface in direct relation to the vesical trigone?
optionExplanations: The posterior lobe is located behind the urethra and inferior to the level of the ejaculatory ducts. It is the primary site for the development of prostatic carcinoma and is easily accessible during a digital rectal examination.

Similar to the right lateral lobe, the left lateral lobe is separated from its counterpart by a shallow vertical groove on the posterior surface and is not the wedge-shaped median structure related to the trigone.

The lateral lobes (right and left) are located on either side of the prostatic urethra and contain the bulk of the gland's glandular tissue, but they do not form the specific wedge related to the trigone and ejaculatory ducts.

The median (or middle) lobe is correctly identified as the glandular wedge located between the urethra and ejaculatory ducts. It is clinically vital because its enlargement in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) projects into the bladder neck and trigone, obstructing urinary flow.

The anterior lobe is situated in front of the prostatic urethra and is distinct for being entirely devoid of glandular tissue, making it clinically insignificant regarding prostatic secretions or hypertrophy.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median (middle) lobe is the wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts. Its upper surface is related to the trigone of the bladder; it is rich in glands.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: When defining the five lobes of the prostate gland, which anatomical structures serve as the primary boundaries for the median (middle) lobe?
options: The prostatic urethra and the ejaculatory ducts
The ejaculatory ducts and the vertical posterior groove
The prostatic urethra and the anterior capsule
The urogenital diaphragm and the apex
The bladder neck and the anterior lobe
correctOption: The prostatic urethra and the ejaculatory ducts
optionExplanations: The median lobe is precisely defined as the wedge of glandular tissue found between the prostatic urethra (anteriorly) and the two ejaculatory ducts (posteriorly).
The vertical posterior groove separates the lateral lobes on the surface; the median lobe is a deeper wedge-shaped internal division.
The anterior lobe is defined as being in front of the urethra; the median lobe is located posterior to the urethra.
The urogenital diaphragm relates to the apex of the entire gland, not the specific boundary of the median lobe.
While the median lobe's upper surface relates to the bladder neck (trigone), its defining boundaries for classification are the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median (middle) lobe is the wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: A 62-year-old male is undergoing surgery for a large prostatic mass. The surgeon notes that the mass has caused the prostatic urethra to become elongated and laterally compressed. Which prostatic lobes, when undergoing benign enlargement, are most typically responsible for this specific urethral distortion?
optionExplanations: The anterior lobe lacks glands and doesn't hypertrophy; the posterior lobe's growth is typically malignant and doesn't initially compress the urethra.
The anterior lobe is not involved in benign prostatic enlargement or the subsequent compression of the urethra.
The lateral lobes cause the 'lateral compression' and the median lobe causes 'elongation' as it grows toward the bladder, combined they distort the lumen.
The posterior lobe rarely contributes to the urinary obstruction seen in classic benign enlargement, which is a feature of the median and lateral lobes.
While the lateral lobes compress the urethra, the posterior lobe is generally not responsible for the obstructive symptoms of BPH.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The enlargement of the median and lateral lobes of the gland produces elongation and lateral compression and distortion of the urethra so that the patient experiences difficulty in passing urine

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a tumor in the posterior lobe of the prostate. Given the lobar anatomy, what is the most significant clinical application of this specific location during a physical examination?
options: It will be obscured by the extraperitoneal fat of the cave of Retzius
It will immediately obstruct the internal urethral sphincter
It will drain directly into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes
It will cause referred pain to the interureteric ridge
It will be palpable as a nodule through the anterior rectal wall
correctOption: It will be palpable as a nodule through the anterior rectal wall
optionExplanations: The cave of Retzius (retropubic space) contains extraperitoneal fat and relates to the anterior surface of the prostate, not the posterior lobe.

Obstruction of the internal sphincter is characteristic of the median lobe (upward enlargement), whereas the posterior lobe is located inferior to the ejaculatory ducts and further from the bladder neck.
The prostate gland (including the posterior lobe) drains to the internal iliac lymph nodes, unlike the scrotum or anal skin which drain to the superficial inguinal nodes.
The interureteric ridge is inside the bladder; prostatic pathology causes symptoms like stagnant urine or urgency, but not specific referred pain to that internal bladder landmark.
The posterior lobe is the part of the gland related to the rectal ampulla, separated only by the rectovesical septum. Therefore, tumors in this lobe are readily palpable during a digital rectal exam.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts... The examiner’s gloved finger can feel the posterior surface of the prostate through the anterior rectal wall.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A patient is identified as having an enlarged 'uvula vesicae' during cystoscopy. This morphological feature is an elevation in the bladder trigone caused by the underlying growth of which prostatic structure?
optionExplanations: The anterior lobe is located in front of the urethra and does not relate to the floor (trigone) of the bladder.
The median lobe is a wedge of tissue between the urethra and ejaculatory ducts; its expansion pushes up against the bladder neck, forming the uvula vesicae.
The posterior lobe is located inferiorly and posteriorly, separated from the bladder trigone by the median lobe and ejaculatory ducts.
The prostatic sinuses are grooves on either side of the urethral crest where prostatic ducts open; they are features of the urethra, not the bladder.
The prostatic utricle is a depression within the prostatic urethra, not a structure that forms an elevation in the bladder trigone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The uvula vesicae are a small elevation situated immediately behind the urethral orifice, which is produced by the underlying median lobe of the prostate.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A 28-year-old male is undergoing physiological testing. During the process of ejaculation, which nervous mechanism is specifically responsible for stimulating the smooth muscle within the prostate to discharge its milky fluid into the urethra?
options: Parasympathetic impulses from the Vagus nerve
Somatic motor fibers from the Pudendal nerve
Sympathetic fibers from the inferior hypogastric plexuses
Parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves
Somatic sensory fibers from the Genitofemoral nerve
correctOption: Sympathetic fibers from the inferior hypogastric plexuses
optionExplanations: The Vagus nerve does not provide motor supply to the pelvic viscera or the reproductive glands.
The Pudendal nerve (S2-S4) provides somatic supply to the skeletal muscles like the bulbospongiosus, not the smooth muscle of the gland.
The sympathetic nervous system, originating from T1-L2 and reaching the gland via the inferior hypogastric plexus, triggers the contraction of prostatic smooth muscle.
The pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic) are primarily involved in the mechanism of penile erection (vasodilation), not the contractile phase of ejaculation.
The Genitofemoral nerve provides sensory supply to the scrotum and motor supply to the cremaster muscle, but not the prostate.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sympathetic nerves stimulate the smooth muscle of the prostate during ejaculation.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
coreConcept: Anatomical orientation for clinical prostatic palpation.
statement: During a digital rectal examination (DRE), which specific part of the prostate gland is primarily evaluated as it lies in direct contact with the anterior rectal wall?
options: Lateral surface of the right lateral lobe
Superior surface of the median lobe
Anterior surface of the anterior lobe
Apex of the prostate resting on the diaphragm
optionExplanations: The lateral surfaces are embraced by the levator ani muscles; while the lateral edges can be reached, the finger primarily rests on the posterior aspect and the median groove between the lateral lobes.

The superior surface (base) is continuous with the bladder neck; it can only be palpated bimanually if the bladder is empty and the finger is pushed very high, but it is not the primary contact point.
The anterior surface of the prostate is related to the pubic symphysis and the cave of Retzius; it is inaccessible to the finger during a rectal examination.
The apex lies inferiorly against the urogenital diaphragm; while it can be felt at the lowest point of the palpation, the entire posterior surface is the focus of the clinical evaluation.
The posterior surface of the prostate gland is separated from the rectum only by the thin rectovesical septum (fascia of Denonvilliers), making it the primary anatomical site palpable via the rectum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The examiner’s gloved finger can feel the posterior surface of the prostate through the anterior rectal wall.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
coreConcept: Mechanistic Basis of Urinary Urgency in BPH
statement: In the clinical progression of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), a specific mechanistic pathway leads to the symptom of intense urinary urgency. Which anatomical change within the prostatic lobes initiates this reflex?
options: Enlargement of the apex against the superior surface of the urogenital diaphragm
Lateral lobe atrophy reducing the tension of the puboprostatic ligaments
Posterior lobe hypertrophy causing mechanical torsion of the ejaculatory ducts
Fibrosis of the anterior lobe compressing the pre-prostatic urethra
Median lobe enlargement encroaching upon the sphincter vesicae
correctOption: Median lobe enlargement encroaching upon the sphincter vesicae
optionExplanations: The apex lies against the urogenital diaphragm, but its enlargement causes distal compression rather than the specific trigger for reflex urgency at the bladder neck.
BPH involves enlargement (hyperplasia), not atrophy. Lateral lobe enlargement causes urethral compression, but urgency is specifically linked to the median lobe's effect on the sphincter vesicae.
The posterior lobe is primarily associated with malignancy rather than the benign obstructive/irritative symptoms resulting from bladder neck encroachment.
The anterior lobe is non-glandular and does not typically undergo the hyperplastic changes associated with the urinary urgency seen in BPH.

Hypertrophy of the median lobe causes it to bulge into the bladder neck (sphincter vesicae). This mechanical disruption allows small amounts of urine to enter the prostatic urethra, which triggers the sensory reflex for micturition.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median lobe of the gland enlarges upward and encroaches within the sphincter vesicae, located at the neck of the bladder (Fig. 9.17). The leakage of urine into the prostatic urethra causes an intense reflex desire to micturate.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: A 75-year-old male presents with urinary retention and severe back pain. Imaging reveals prostatic enlargement and osteoblastic metastasis in the vertebrae. While the urinary retention is caused by lateral and median lobe hypertrophy, the vertebral metastasis most likely originated from a primary tumor in which lobe via the prostatic venous plexus?
optionExplanations: Lateral lobes contribute significantly to BPH-induced obstruction but are less common primary sites for early cancer than the posterior lobe.
The median lobe is more commonly associated with benign hyperplasia and obstruction rather than early-stage asymptomatic cancer spread.
There is no 'internal' lobe in the standard five-lobe anatomical classification of the prostate.
The posterior lobe is the most common site for prostatic cancer. Cells can enter the valveless prostatic venous plexus and reach the vertebral veins, leading to skeletal metastases.
The anterior lobe is non-glandular and rarely the site of primary prostatic carcinoma.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts... This explains the frequent occurrence of skeletal metastases in the lower vertebral column.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A medical student is performing a digital rectal examination (DRE) on a patient. Which specific surface of the prostate gland is the student palpating through the anterior wall of the rectal ampulla?
optionExplanations: The posterior surface of the prostate gland is in direct contact with the rectovesical septum and the anterior wall of the rectum, making it the only surface palpated during a DRE.
The apex of the prostate lies inferiorly against the urogenital diaphragm and is less accessible than the broad posterior surface.
The superior surface is synonymous with the base, which is related to the bladder and not accessible via DRE.
The base of the prostate is superior and continuous with the bladder neck; it is further away from the anal canal.
The anterior surface faces the symphysis pubis and cannot be palpated via the rectum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The examiner’s gloved finger can feel the posterior surface of the prostate through the anterior rectal wall.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: According to the anatomical subdivisions of the prostate, which lobe is specifically defined by its location between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts?
optionExplanations: The anterior lobe is located strictly in front of the urethra.
There is no lobe formally classified as the 'Superior lobe' in the five-lobe classification system; the base of the gland is the superior portion.
The median lobe is anatomically defined as the wedge-shaped portion of the prostate located between the urethra (anteriorly) and the ejaculatory ducts (posteriorly).
The lateral lobes are situated on either side of the urethra, not specifically between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts.
The posterior lobe is located behind the urethra and below (inferior to) the ejaculatory ducts.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median (middle) lobe is the wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: A 72-year-old male with confirmed early-stage prostatic carcinoma has a malignant focus localized strictly to the posterior lobe. Despite the malignancy, he has no abnormal urinary symptoms. What anatomical relationship of the posterior lobe explains the absence of urinary obstruction in this case?
options: It is separated from the urethra by the two lateral lobes.
It is located superior to the trigone of the bladder.
It is devoid of glandular tissue, preventing expansion.
It is continuous with the neck of the bladder and expands away from the lumen.
It is situated behind the urethra and below the level of the ejaculatory ducts.
correctOption: It is situated behind the urethra and below the level of the ejaculatory ducts.
optionExplanations: The lateral lobes are on either side of the urethra, but they do not separate the posterior lobe from the urethra; they are simply adjacent anatomical divisions.
The median lobe relates to the trigone, not the posterior lobe; a posterior location below the ejaculatory ducts avoids early urethral compression.
The anterior lobe is devoid of glandular tissue, not the posterior lobe; the posterior lobe is rich in glands and is the common site for cancer.
The base of the prostate (median and lateral lobes) is continuous with the bladder neck; the posterior lobe is inferior-posterior and does not surround the bladder neck.

Because the posterior lobe is located behind the urethra and specifically below the level of the ejaculatory ducts, it can harbor a tumor without initially compressing the prostatic urethra or the bladder neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts and also contains glandular tissue. ... The patient was very upset, especially because he had no abnormal urinary symptoms.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: The prostate gland is described as a fibromuscular glandular organ. During ejaculation, what specific mechanism ensures that the prostatic secretions are squeezed into the prostatic urethra?
options: Contraction of the smooth muscle surrounding the glands
Passive drainage from the prostatic sinuses
Contraction of the levator ani fibers
Contraction of the skeletal muscle of the urogenital diaphragm
correctOption: Contraction of the smooth muscle surrounding the glands
optionExplanations: The prostatic stroma contains abundant smooth muscle; sympathetic stimulation during ejaculation causes this muscle to contract and expel fluid.
Relaxation of the sphincter vesicae occurs during micturition; during ejaculation, it actually contracts to prevent retrograde flow.
The drainage is active, not passive, mediated by the fibromuscular stroma under autonomic control.
The levator ani (anterior fibers) embraces the prostate laterally but does not mediate the internal glandular discharge.
The urogenital diaphragm supports the apex but is skeletal muscle not responsible for squeezing the internal prostatic glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The smooth muscle, which surrounds the glands, squeezes the secretion into the prostatic urethra.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: During a digital rectal examination, a clinician identifies a hard, irregular nodule. Contrast this finding with the typical clinical presentation of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) regarding its anatomical site of origin.
options: BPH originates in the posterior lobe, while carcinoma arises in the anterior fibromuscular stroma.
BPH originates in the anterior lobe, while carcinoma originates in the lateral lobes.
BPH involves the ejaculatory ducts, while carcinoma involves the prostatic utricle.
BPH involves the apex, while carcinoma involves the base exclusively.
BPH originates in the median and lateral lobes, while carcinoma commonly arises in the posterior lobe.
correctOption: BPH originates in the median and lateral lobes, while carcinoma commonly arises in the posterior lobe.
optionExplanations: The posterior lobe is the classic site for cancer, not BPH; the anterior stroma is rarely involved in these pathological processes.
The anterior lobe is non-glandular and rarely the primary site of either BPH or carcinoma.
The ejaculatory ducts and prostatic utricle are internal landmarks and conduits; they are not the primary sites of origin for these disease states.
Both BPH and carcinoma can affect various levels of the gland; they are not restricted exclusively to the apex or base.

Benign enlargement typically involves the median and lateral lobes, causing urethral obstruction. In contrast, malignancy frequently manifests as a hard nodule on the posterior surface (posterior lobe), which is easily palpable against the rectum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The enlargement of the median and lateral lobes of the gland produces elongation and lateral compression and distortion of the urethra... carcinoma of the prostate... is later confirmed by a needle biopsy of prostatic tissue through the anterior wall of the rectum.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: A 65-year-old patient is diagnosed with carcinoma of the prostate originating in the posterior lobe. During surgery, the surgeon notes that the malignancy has not yet invaded the rectum. Which embryological event is responsible for creating the fascial barrier that initially restricts this spread?
options: The fusion of the lateral labioscrotal swellings
The absorption of the mesonephric ducts into the bladder
The fusion of the walls of the lower end of the rectovesical pouch
The canalization of the vaginal plate
The failure of the mesenchyme to invade the embryonic disc
correctOption: The fusion of the walls of the lower end of the rectovesical pouch
optionExplanations: Fusion of labioscrotal swellings forms the scrotum, which is external anatomy.
Absorption of the mesonephric ducts forms the bladder trigone and has no role in the posterior fascial planes.

The rectovesical septum (Denonvilliers' fascia) is formed when the two walls of the embryological rectovesical pouch of peritoneum fuse. This creates a strong fibrous barrier between the posterior lobe of the prostate and the rectum.
Canalization of the vaginal plate is a female embryological process forming the vaginal lumen.
Failure of mesenchyme to invade the embryonic disc refers to the etiology of exstrophy of the bladder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Posteriorly: The prostate... is separated from it by the rectovesical septum (fascia of Denonvilliers). This septum forms in fetal life by the fusion of the walls of the lower end of the rectovesical pouch of peritoneum, which originally extended down to the perineal body.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
coreConcept: Lobular anatomy and tissue composition of the prostate.
statement: Which specific lobe of the prostate gland is characterized by a lack of glandular tissue and is located anterior to the prostatic urethra?
optionExplanations: The anterior lobe, also known as the isthmus, is unique because it lies directly in front of the prostatic urethra and consists almost entirely of fibromuscular tissue rather than secretory glands.
The left lateral lobe, like its right counterpart, is rich in glandular tissue and is typically separated from the other lateral lobe by a shallow vertical groove on the posterior surface.
The median lobe is a wedge-shaped segment situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts; it is rich in glandular tissue and frequently involved in benign hypertrophy.
The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts; it is highly glandular and is the most common site for primary prostatic carcinoma.
The right lateral lobe is one of the two large masses situated on either side of the urethra; it contains abundant glandular tissue contributing to prostatic secretions.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and is devoid of glandular tissue.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: A clinician compares the clinical presentation of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostatic carcinoma. What is the most characteristic anatomical contrast between these conditions regarding their primary site of origin?
options: BPH starts in the glandular apex, while carcinoma starts in the fibromuscular base.
BPH involves the lateral and median lobes, while carcinoma commonly arises in the posterior lobe.
BPH originates in the anterior lobe, while carcinoma originates in the lateral lobes.
BPH originates in the posterior lobe, while carcinoma is restricted to the median lobe.
BPH arises from the prostatic utricle, while carcinoma arises from the urethral crest.
correctOption: BPH involves the lateral and median lobes, while carcinoma commonly arises in the posterior lobe.
optionExplanations: Prostatic disease is classified by lobes/zones rather than a simple apex/base division; BPH involves specific glandular lobes, not the entire apex.
BPH typically causes symptoms via median and lateral lobe hypertrophy, whereas cancer is famously detected as a nodule in the posterior lobe during rectal exams.
The anterior lobe is devoid of glandular tissue and is rarely the site of BPH or carcinoma.
This reverses the classic sites; the posterior lobe is the classic site for malignancy, not BPH.
Neither condition originates from these specific small landmarks on the urethral crest.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Benign enlargement of the prostate is common in men older than 50 years. The cause is possibly an imbalance in the hormonal control of the gland. The median lobe of the gland enlarges upward... The enlargement of the median and lateral lobes of the gland produces elongation and lateral compression... carcinoma of the prostate [presents as] a small, hard nodule projecting from the posterior surface.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: A 72-year-old male presents with chronic lower back pain and urinary frequency. A digital rectal examination reveals a hard, irregular nodule on the posterior surface of the prostate. Imaging confirms metastatic deposits in the lower lumbar vertebrae. Through which anatomical route did the malignant cells most likely travel to reach the vertebral column?
options: Prostatic venous plexus to vertebral veins
correctOption: Prostatic venous plexus to vertebral veins
optionExplanations: The obturator nerve sheath is not a recognized vascular or lymphatic pathway for prostatic malignancy spread.
The internal pudendal artery provides arterial supply to the perineum but is not a primary route for venous/metastatic spread to the spine.
The inferior vesical artery provides oxygenated blood to the prostate and is not used for the embolic spread of cancer cells to the spine.

The prostatic venous plexus is valveless and communicates directly with the vertebral venous plexus. Increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., coughing) allows blood/cancer cells to flow retrogressively into the vertebral veins.
While the internal iliac nodes receive lymph from the prostate, they would lead to lymphatic spread rather than the direct skeletal spread described in the vertebral column.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Many connections exist between the prostatic venous plexus and the vertebral veins... This explains the frequent occurrence of skeletal metastases in the lower vertebral column and pelvic bones of patients with carcinoma of the prostate.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: The prostate gland secretes a thin, milky fluid containing acid phosphatase and citric acid. During the physiological step of ejaculation, this secretion is squeezed into the urethra. Based on the internal anatomy, into which specific urethral structure do the ducts of the glandular lobes primarily discharge?
optionExplanations: The urethral crest is the longitudinal ridge on the posterior wall, but the glandular ducts open into the grooves flanking it, not the summit of the crest itself.
The ejaculatory ducts have their own specific openings on the margins of the prostatic utricle; they transport semen from the seminal vesicles and vasa deferentia, not the prostatic fluid itself.
The fossa terminalis (navicular fossa) is located within the glans penis at the distal end of the penile urethra, far from the prostatic lobe drainage sites.
The prostatic utricle is a blind-ending central depression on the urethral crest; it does not receive the bulk of the prostatic glandular secretions.

The numerous ducts from the lateral and median lobes terminate in the prostatic sinuses, which are longitudinal grooves located on either side of the urethral crest on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A groove called the prostatic sinus runs along each side of the crest; the prostatic glands open into these grooves.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: A clinician compares the clinical findings of benign prostatic enlargement with early prostatic carcinoma. Which anatomical lobe correlation correctly differentiates these two conditions during a physical examination?
options: Malignancy is confined to the fibromuscular anterior lobe, while BPH is confined to the posterior lobe.
Malignancy typically presents as a hard nodule on the posterior lobe, while BPH involves the median and lateral lobes.
BPH involves only the right lateral lobe, while malignancy involves only the left lateral lobe.
BPH typically presents as a nodule on the anterior lobe, while malignancy involves the ejaculatory ducts.
Malignancy causes encroachment of the sphincter vesicae, while BPH remains localized to the rectovesical septum.
correctOption: Malignancy typically presents as a hard nodule on the posterior lobe, while BPH involves the median and lateral lobes.
optionExplanations: Carcinoma rarely begins in the anterior lobe due to its lack of glandular tissue, and BPH is never confined solely to the posterior lobe.

Primary carcinoma of the prostate most frequently arises in the posterior lobe, which is why it is palpable as a hard nodule during a digital rectal exam. Conversely, BPH usually involves the median and lateral lobes, leading to urethral compression symptoms.
Both BPH and malignancy can be bilateral or involve multiple lobes; they are not restricted to just one lateral lobe based on the disease process.
BPH does not typically involve the anterior lobe because that lobe is devoid of glandular tissue; it primarily affects the mucosal and submucosal glands of the median and lateral lobes.
Encroachment of the sphincter vesicae is a classic manifestation of median lobe BPH, not malignancy, which tends to stay in the posterior zone for a longer period before invading the bladder neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The physician found a small, hard nodule projecting from the posterior surface of the prostate gland... The diagnosis was early cancer of the prostate... Benign enlargement of the prostate... The median and lateral lobes of the gland produces elongation and lateral compression and distortion of the urethra.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
coreConcept: Lobe-Specific Clinical Presentation of Prostatic Cancer
statement: A 66-year-old male undergoes a physical for lower back pain. Rectal exam reveals a small, hard, fixed nodule on the prostate's posterior surface. PSA is 18 ng/mL, but he reports no urinary frequency or weak stream. Anatomically, why can malignancy in this specific lobe progress significantly before causing obstructive voiding symptoms?
options: It is situated anterior to the urethra, allowing expansion away from the lumen
It is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts, distal to the sphincter vesicae
It consists of fibromuscular tissue that does not compress the urethral wall
It is separated from the prostatic urethra by the median and lateral lobes
It is located superior to the bladder neck
correctOption: It is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts, distal to the sphincter vesicae
optionExplanations: The anterior lobe is in front of the urethra but rarely hosts malignancy due to its non-glandular nature.

Cancer typically arises in the posterior lobe. Because this lobe is behind the urethra and below the level of the ejaculatory ducts and bladder neck, it can expand significantly without compressing the urethral lumen early in the disease.
The posterior lobe is glandular, which is why it is a common site for adenocarcinoma; it is not purely fibromuscular.

The posterior lobe is adjacent to the urethra posteriorly; it isn't separated by other lobes, but its position distal to the internal sphincter prevents early obstructive symptoms compared to the median lobe.
The prostate is inferior to the bladder neck; no lobe is superior to it.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts... knowledge of the relevant anatomic features of the pelvis can recognize an abnormal prostate when it is palpated through the anterior rectal wall.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: During the physiological process of ejaculation, the prostate gland must discharge its secretions into the prostatic urethra. This is facilitated by the autonomic nervous system. What is the specific neurovascular mechanism involved?
options: Parasympathetic stimulation of prostatic glandular epithelium
Sympathetic stimulation causing contraction of smooth muscle in the gland's stroma
Sympathetic inhibition of the internal urethral sphincter
Somatic motor impulses from the pudendal nerve to the bulbospongiosus
Nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation of helicine arteries
correctOption: Sympathetic stimulation causing contraction of smooth muscle in the gland's stroma
optionExplanations: Parasympathetic fibers primarily control penile erection via vasodilation, not the mechanical emptying of the prostate during ejaculation.
Sympathetic nerves from the inferior hypogastric plexus trigger the contraction of smooth muscle fibers embedded within the prostatic stroma, squeezing fluid into the urethra.
During ejaculation, the sympathetic system actually contracts the internal urethral sphincter to prevent retrograde ejaculation into the bladder.
The pudendal nerve controls skeletal muscles like the bulbospongiosus for ejection of semen, but the initial 'emission' from the prostate is sympathetic.
Nitric oxide and helicine artery dilation are mechanisms specific to penile erection, not prostatic secretion discharge.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sympathetic nerves stimulate the smooth muscle of the prostate during ejaculation.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
coreConcept: Clinical Topography of the Prostate on DRE
statement: During a digital rectal examination (DRE), which prostatic structure produces the palpable vertical groove that clinicians use to orient themselves and assess for symmetry?
options: The interureteric ridge on the bladder trigone
The puboprostatic ligament attached to the pubis
The urethral crest on the posterior wall of the urethra
The vertical groove separating the two lateral lobes
The median umbilical ligament extending from the apex
correctOption: The vertical groove separating the two lateral lobes
optionExplanations: The interureteric ridge is inside the bladder trigone and cannot be felt during a standard rectal exam of the prostate.
Puboprostatic ligaments are anterior structures connecting the prostate to the pubic bones, making them inaccessible during DRE.
The urethral crest is an internal feature of the posterior urethral wall and is not directly palpable as an external groove during a DRE.

The posterior surface of the prostate, felt through the rectum, has a midline sulcus (groove) that separates the bulky lateral lobes. Disappearance of this groove can indicate hyperplasia or malignancy.
The median umbilical ligament is an anterior abdominal structure and is not related to the palpable posterior surface of the prostate.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The right and left lateral lobes lie on either side of the urethra and are separated from one another by a shallow vertical groove on the posterior surface of the prostate.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
coreConcept: Median Lobe Enlargement and Urinary Stasis
statement: A 70-year-old male presents with urinary frequency, urgency, and a sensation of incomplete emptying. Cystoscopy reveals an enlarged uvula vesicae and a pouch of stagnant urine behind the internal urethral orifice. Which prostatic lobe is primarily responsible for these specific findings at the bladder neck?
optionExplanations: The posterior lobe is located inferior to the ejaculatory ducts and does not project into the trigone area to form a stagnant urine pouch.
While lateral lobes contribute to urethral compression, they do not form the uvula vesicae or the specific pouching behind the urethral orifice.
The left lateral lobe, like the right, causes lateral compression of the urethra but is not responsible for the apical bladder neck changes seen in this patient.
The median lobe is the only lobe that enlarges upward into the sphincter vesicae, elevating the uvula vesicae and creating a retro-urethral pouch where urine stagnates.
The anterior lobe does not contain glandular tissue and is not associated with the formation of the uvula vesicae or bladder neck obstruction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The enlargement of the uvula vesicae (owing to the enlarged median lobe) results in the formation of a pouch of stagnant urine behind the urethral orifice within the bladder.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
coreConcept: The Batson venous plexus and the retrograde metastatic pathway of prostatic cancer.
statement: A patient with carcinoma of the prostate presents with new-onset back pain. Considering the neurovascular supply of the gland, which anatomical mechanism facilitates the retrograde spread of malignant cells to the lower vertebral column during acts of abdominal straining?
options: Lymphatic spread via the external iliac nodes to the lumbar chain
Sympathetic fiber conduction through the inferior hypogastric plexus
Drainage through the internal pudendal vein to the caval system
Reverse flow through valveless connections between the prostatic and vertebral venous plexuses
Direct arterial embolization via the inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries
correctOption: Reverse flow through valveless connections between the prostatic and vertebral venous plexuses
optionExplanations: The prostate drains primarily to the internal iliac nodes. While lymphatic spread occurs, the rapid and specific involvement of the vertebral column is classically attributed to the valveless venous plexus connections.

The inferior hypogastric plexus provides the autonomic (sympathetic) supply responsible for smooth muscle contraction during ejaculation; however, nerves do not serve as conduits for the physical migration of malignant cell masses to the skeleton.

While the prostatic plexus eventually drains into the internal iliac system (to which the internal pudendal is related), this systemic route does not directly explain the specific, high-frequency localization to the vertebrae compared to the Batson plexus pathway.

The prostatic venous plexus is valveless and maintains numerous communications with the vertebral (Batson's) plexus. Increases in intra-abdominal pressure (straining, coughing) cause blood to flow backward into the vertebral veins, carrying cancer cells directly to the bones of the spine.

The inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries provide the primary blood supply to the prostate, but arterial spread is a less common mechanism for initial localized skeletal metastasis compared to the specialized venous connections.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Many connections exist between the prostatic venous plexus and the vertebral veins. During coughing and sneezing or abdominal straining, it is possible for prostatic venous blood to flow in a reverse direction and enter the vertebral veins. This explains the frequent occurrence of skeletal metastases in the lower vertebral column and pelvic bones

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a hard nodule on the prostate that is palpable via the anterior rectal wall. Based on its location relative to the ejaculatory ducts and its clinical accessibility via DRE, which lobe is most likely the site of this pathology?
optionExplanations: The posterior lobe lies behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts, making it the most posterior part of the gland and the specific area directly accessible to the finger during a digital rectal exam.
The anterior lobe is separated from the rectum by the urethra and the entire mass of the prostate, making it impossible to palpate via DRE.
The right lateral lobe, like the left, is lateral to the midline; the primary posterior surface is clinically defined as the posterior lobe.
The median lobe is located superiorly and centrally; while it can bulge into the bladder, it is not the primary surface felt on the posterior aspect during a standard DRE.

The lateral lobes are located on the sides; while the posterior part of the lateral lobes may be felt, the nodule described is typical of the posterior lobe, which is the classic site for palpable cancer.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts... The examiner’s gloved finger can feel the posterior surface of the prostate through the anterior rectal wall.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
coreConcept: Median Lobe and Irritative Urinary Symptoms
statement: A 68-year-old male with confirmed BPH reports an 'intense reflex desire' to urinate even with very small volumes of urine. This specific symptom is caused by urine leakage into the prostatic urethra due to the encroachment of which prostatic lobe upon the internal urethral sphincter?
optionExplanations: The left lateral lobe causes obstructive symptoms (weak stream) via urethral compression but is not the primary cause of sphincter encroachment.
The anterior lobe is devoid of glandular tissue and does not undergo the hyperplasia that leads to BPH symptoms.
The posterior lobe is located below the bladder neck and does not interfere with the sphincter vesicae mechanisms.
The median lobe is uniquely positioned to enlarge upward and disrupt the sphincter vesicae, allowing urine to enter the sensitive prostatic urethra and trigger the voiding reflex.
While the lateral lobes compress the urethra laterally, they do not specifically enlarge upward into the internal sphincter.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median lobe of the gland enlarges upward and encroaches within the sphincter vesicae... The leakage of urine into the prostatic urethra causes an intense reflex desire to micturate.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
coreConcept: Prostatic Surface Anatomy and Lobe Boundaries
statement: A clinician performing a digital rectal examination notes a shallow vertical groove on the posterior aspect of the prostate. Which anatomical landmark or boundary is primarily defined by this groove?
options: The separation between the two lateral lobes
The separation between the median and posterior lobes
The junction of the prostate apex and the urogenital diaphragm
The boundary between the anterior and median lobes
The entry point of the ejaculatory ducts into the gland
correctOption: The separation between the two lateral lobes
optionExplanations: The right and left lateral lobes are the primary glandular masses on the sides of the urethra. On the posterior surface, they are demarcated by a palpable shallow vertical groove.
The median lobe is a deeper wedge between the urethra and ejaculatory ducts; the posterior groove is a surface feature separating the lateral masses.
The apex-diaphragm junction is the inferior-most limit of the prostate, whereas the vertical groove is on the posterior rectal surface of the gland's body.
The anterior lobe is on the opposite side of the gland from the posterior surface, making it impossible for a posterior groove to define its boundary with the median lobe.
The ejaculatory ducts pierce the upper part of the posterior surface but do not define the vertical groove; the groove is a longitudinal feature of the lateral lobes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The right and left lateral lobes lie on either side of the urethra and are separated from one another by a shallow vertical groove on the posterior surface of the prostate.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: Anatomical study of the prostate gland reveals distinct lobar divisions with varying tissue compositions. Which specific lobe is characterized by a complete absence of glandular tissue?
optionExplanations: The left lateral lobe, like its right-sided counterpart, is rich in glandular tissue.
The median (middle) lobe is a wedge of gland situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts; it is actually very rich in glands, unlike the anterior lobe.
The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts and contains glandular tissue, making it a frequent site for pathology.
The right lateral lobe is situated on the side of the urethra and contains many glands.
The anterior lobe is a distinct anatomical region lying in front of the urethra. It is unique among the prostatic lobes because it is entirely fibromuscular and devoid of glandular elements.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and is devoid of glandular tissue.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with urinary frequency and an intense, repetitive reflex desire to micturate. Pathophysiologically, this specific clinical manifestation is most directly attributed to which lobe-specific change during benign prostatic enlargement?
options: Lateral lobe elongation of the membranous urethra
Median lobe encroachment on the sphincter vesicae
Lateral lobe compression of the fossa terminalis
correctOption: Median lobe encroachment on the sphincter vesicae
optionExplanations: The anterior lobe is devoid of glandular tissue and its involvement in hypertrophy is minimal compared to the median and lateral lobes.
Posterior lobe nodules are more typical of malignancy and usually do not cause early irritative symptoms like reflex desire to micturate unless they invade the bladder neck.
While lateral lobes compress the prostatic urethra, they do not typically elongate the membranous (intermediate) urethra, which is fixed within the urogenital diaphragm.

When the median lobe enlarges upward, it disrupts the integrity of the sphincter vesicae at the bladder neck. This allows urine to leak into the sensitive prostatic urethra, triggering a persistent and intense reflex urge to void.
The fossa terminalis is located within the glans penis, far distal to the lateral lobes of the prostate, and is not compressed by prostatic enlargement.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median lobe of the gland enlarges upward and encroaches within the sphincter vesicae... The leakage of urine into the prostatic urethra causes an intense reflex desire to micturate.

category: Describe the morphological features and neurovascular supply of prostate
statement: During a digital rectal examination, which morphological feature of the prostate is specifically palpated through the anterior rectal wall to assess for malignancy?
optionExplanations: The posterior surface of the prostate is closely related to the anterior surface of the rectal ampulla, separated only by the rectovesical septum. This makes it the only surface accessible for clinical palpation.
The anterior lobe is situated behind the symphysis pubis and in front of the urethra, making it inaccessible to palpation via the rectum.
The median lobe is located deep within the gland between the urethra and ejaculatory ducts and cannot be directly felt during a standard digital rectal exam.
The prostatic utricle is a microscopic internal depression on the urethral crest within the prostatic urethra and is not a palpable external surface feature.
The apex of the prostate lies inferiorly against the urogenital diaphragm; while it can be reached, the clinician specifically assesses the broad posterior surface for nodules.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The examiner’s gloved finger can feel the posterior surface of the prostate through the anterior rectal wall.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: Anatomical examination of the prostate gland reveals one specific lobe that is distinct because it is completely devoid of glandular tissue. Which of the following is that lobe?
optionExplanations: The anterior lobe is unique among the five prostatic lobes because it is fibro-muscular in nature and lacks the glandular acini responsible for prostatic secretions, serving primarily as a structural part of the gland in front of the urethra.
The right lateral lobe is one of the two largest lobes of the gland, containing high concentrations of glandular tissue and separated from the left lobe by a posterior vertical groove.
The median (middle) lobe is a wedge of tissue situated between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts; it is rich in glandular tissue and its enlargement is a primary cause of urinary obstruction.
The left lateral lobe, like its right counterpart, is highly glandular and forms the bulk of the lateral mass of the prostate on either side of the urethra.
The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts; it contains significant glandular tissue and is a common site for the development of prostatic carcinoma.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and is devoid of glandular tissue.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: In the internal anatomy of the bladder and prostate, a small elevation known as the uvula vesicae is formed by the projection of an underlying prostatic lobe. Which lobe is responsible for this landmark in the bladder trigone?
optionExplanations: The median lobe's upper surface is related directly to the bladder trigone, and its projection creates the uvula vesicae elevation.
The anterior lobe lies in front of the urethra and has no relation to the posterior bladder trigone or the uvula vesicae.
The posterior lobe is below the level of the bladder neck and ejaculatory ducts, preventing it from forming the uvula vesicae.
The right lateral lobe is on the side of the urethra and does not project into the midline bladder orifice to form the uvula.
The left lateral lobe, like the right, is lateral to the midline and does not contribute to the uvula vesicae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The uvula vesicae are a small elevation situated immediately behind the urethral orifice, which is produced by the underlying median lobe of the prostate.

category: Correlate the clinical manifestations of prostate with lobes and/or zones of prostate
coreConcept: Asymptomatic Nature of Early Prostate Cancer
statement: A 62-year-old male is diagnosed with early prostatic cancer after a hard nodule is felt during a rectal exam. He is surprised that he has no urinary symptoms. Based on the anatomical relations of the prostate, why is early cancer often asymptomatic regarding urination?
options: Prostatic cancer secretions are acidic and neutralize the normally alkaline urine, preventing irritation.
Early malignancy causes the prostatic urethra to dilate rather than compress.
The cancer cells initially only involve the non-glandular fibromuscular stroma.
Cancer typically arises in the anterior lobe, which is distant from the bladder neck.
The posterior lobe, where cancer often starts, is situated away from the urethral lumen and ejaculatory ducts.
correctOption: The posterior lobe, where cancer often starts, is situated away from the urethral lumen and ejaculatory ducts.
optionExplanations: There is no physiological evidence that cancer secretions neutralize urine to prevent symptoms; the absence of symptoms is purely anatomical.
Malignancy eventually causes compression and invasion, never dilation, of the prostatic urethra.
Malignancy arises from the glandular epithelial cells, not the stroma, and its lack of symptoms is due to location, not the type of tissue involved.
The anterior lobe is actually in front of the urethra; however, cancer rarely originates there because it is devoid of glandular tissue.

Early prostatic carcinoma usually develops in the posterior lobe. Because this lobe is located behind the urethra and below the level of the ejaculatory ducts, a tumor can grow significantly before it causes any mechanical compression or distortion of the urethra, leaving the patient asymptomatic.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The physician found a small, hard nodule projecting from the posterior surface of the prostate gland... The patient was very upset, especially because he had no abnormal urinary symptoms... The posterior lobe is situated behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts.

category: Describe, Draw & Label Lobes of prostate gland
statement: The median (middle) lobe of the prostate gland is a critical wedge of tissue. Which anatomical relationship accurately defines its superior boundary?
options: Its upper surface is related to the trigone of the bladder.
It is separated from the bladder by the rectovesical septum.
It is related to the urogenital diaphragm.
It is bounded superiorly by the pubic symphysis.
It is related to the apex of the prostate.
correctOption: Its upper surface is related to the trigone of the bladder.
optionExplanations: Correct. The median lobe sits as a wedge between the urethra and ejaculatory ducts, with its superior aspect lying just deep to the trigone of the urinary bladder.
The rectovesical septum (Denonvilliers' fascia) separates the posterior surface of the prostate from the rectum, not the median lobe from the bladder.
The urogenital diaphragm relates to the apex of the prostate, not the superiorly placed median lobe.
